newsitem.title: FRANCE: DUTCH GDP GROWTH TO ACCELERATE TO THREE PCT - OECD.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH GDP GROWTH TO ACCELERATE TO THREE PCT - OECD.

text.p: Dutch GDP growth will accelerate to a rate of about three percent in 1998 with exports initially taking over from consumer spending as the driving force behind the economy, the OECD said in its twice-yearly Economic Outlook.
"Supported initially by a pick-up in foreign demand, GDP growth is projected to accelerate slightly over the next two years, reaching three percent in 1998," the OECD said.
However, the foreign balance was likely to make a smaller contribution to overall growth in 1998 because of reduced export competitiveness and a strengthening of domestic demand, it said.
"Consumer demand may lose some buoyancy in 1997 before picking up again in 1998, following a similar pattern in disposable income," the Paris-based organisation said.
The growth of business investment was expected to accelerate, spurred on by high rates of capacity utilisation and improved profitability.
But the Netherlands would also face higher levels of inflation, the OECD added.
"With the economy reaching its potential and labour market conditions tightening, some inflationary pressures are likely to arise," the organisation said.
Wage increases might pick up to three percent while consumer price inflation could edge up to 2.25 percent in 1998, it said.
The OECD said the Dutch economy had rebounded in 1996 after only a shallow downturn in 1995 as improving confidence and robust employment growth led to strong consumer spending.
Dutch GDP growth for 1996, at around 2.75 percent, may have been substantially higher than the EU average, it said.

The OECD said growth of disposable incomes would not be strong enough to sustain high levels of consumer spending in 1997-98. However, this would be offset by an economic upturn in neighbouring countries which would boost exports.
Unemployment was likely to continue falling to a rate of around 5.8 percent in 1998, the OECD said.
Short-term interest rates might start to rise in the second half of 1997 but long-term rates might on average be a little lower in 1997-98 than in 1996, it added.
